name: physics_set3_p1
label: Physics: set 3 (waves, sound, light and optics)

papers.title: Wave Motion and Properties: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on wave motion and properties, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 4 m. What is its speed?
questions.explanation:
$v = f\lambda = 50 \times 4 = 200\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 12.5 m s⁻¹: You divided the frequency by the wavelength; $v = f\lambda$.
- 0.08 m s⁻¹: You divided the wavelength by the frequency.
- 54 m s⁻¹: You added the frequency and the wavelength.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a longitudinal wave?
questions.explanation:
In sound, air particles vibrate along the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- light wave: Light is an electromagnetic wave, which is transverse.
- water ripple: Water ripples are (mainly) transverse.
- radio wave: Radio waves are electromagnetic and transverse.

questions.stem: A wave completes 25 oscillations in 5 s. What is its period?
questions.explanation:
$f = \dfrac{25}{5} = 5$ Hz, so $T = \dfrac{1}{f} = 0.2\ \text{s}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5 s: That is the frequency (25 ÷ 5), not the period.
- 125 s: You multiplied the number of oscillations by the time.
- 25 s: That is the number of oscillations, not the time for one.

questions.stem: When a wave passes from one medium into another, the quantity that does NOT change is its
questions.explanation:
The frequency is set by the source, so it stays the same in every medium.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- speed: The speed depends on the medium.
- wavelength: The wavelength changes with the speed ($\lambda = v/f$).
- direction (in general): The direction usually changes: that is refraction.

questions.stem: An FM radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz. What is the wavelength of its waves? (speed of radio waves = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
$\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.0 \times 10^{8}} = 3\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.333 m: You divided the frequency by the speed.
- 3000000 m: You used 100 Hz instead of 100 MHz (100 × 10⁶ Hz).
- 300 m: You used 1 MHz instead of 100 MHz.

questions.stem: The distance between two successive crests of a transverse wave is the
questions.explanation:
Crest to crest (or compression to compression) is one wavelength.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- amplitude: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position.
- frequency: Frequency is the number of waves per second.
- period: Period is a time, not a distance.

questions.stem: Two points on a wave are 0.5 m apart. The wavelength is 2 m. What is the phase difference between them?
questions.explanation:
$\phi = \dfrac{x}{\lambda} \times 360° = \dfrac{0.5}{2} \times 360° = 90°$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 180 °: Points half a wavelength (1 m) apart differ by 180°.
- 45 °: Phase difference = (0.5 ÷ 2) × 360°, not × 180°.
- 360 °: Points one wavelength apart are in phase (360°).

questions.stem: A progressive wave is given by y = 0.02 sin(40πt − 0.5πx) in SI units. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation:
Compare with $y = a\sin(2\pi f t - kx)$: $2\pi f = 40\pi \Rightarrow f = 20\ \text{Hz}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 40 Hz: The coefficient of t is 2πf = 40π, so f = 20 Hz, not 40.
- 125.7 Hz: That is the angular frequency ω in rad s⁻¹.
- 4 Hz: That is the wavelength (2π/0.5π = 4 m).

papers.title: Wave Phenomena: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on wave phenomena, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which wave phenomenon shows that light is a transverse wave?
questions.explanation:
Only transverse waves can be polarised.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- diffraction: All waves, longitudinal ones included, can be diffracted.
- refraction: All waves can be refracted.
- interference: All waves can interfere.

questions.stem: Diffraction of waves through a gap is greatest when the width of the gap is
questions.explanation:
Spreading is greatest when the gap is comparable with the wavelength.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- much larger than the wavelength: A wide gap lets waves through with little spreading.
- twice the amplitude: Amplitude does not decide diffraction.
- zero: With no gap, no waves pass through.

options.label: D
options.content: about the same as the wavelength

questions.stem: When water waves pass from deep to shallow water, their
questions.explanation:
In shallow water the waves slow down; with the frequency fixed, the wavelength gets shorter.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- speed increases and wavelength decreases: Waves slow down in shallow water.
- frequency and speed both decrease: The frequency stays the same.
- wavelength increases and frequency decreases: Both statements are wrong: λ decreases and f is unchanged.

options.label: A
options.content: speed and wavelength decrease but frequency is unchanged

questions.stem: Nodes in a stationary wave are 15 cm apart. What is the wavelength of the wave?
questions.explanation:
Node-to-node distance $= \dfrac{\lambda}{2} = 15$ cm, so $\lambda = 30$ cm.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 15 cm: Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart.
- 7.5 cm: You halved instead of doubling.
- 60 cm: Node to node is λ/2, not λ/4.

questions.stem: Two sources are said to be coherent if they have
questions.explanation:
Coherent sources keep a constant phase difference, which requires the same frequency.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the same amplitude only: Equal amplitudes help, but coherence needs the same frequency and a fixed phase relation.
- different frequencies: Different frequencies cannot give a steady interference pattern.
- the same speed only: Waves in the same medium have the same speed anyway.

options.label: D
options.content: the same frequency and a constant phase difference

questions.stem: Destructive interference occurs at a point where two waves from coherent sources arrive
questions.explanation:
Crest on trough cancels: a path difference of half a wavelength (or 3/2, 5/2, …).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- in phase (crest meeting crest): That gives constructive interference.
- with a path difference of one whole wavelength: That gives constructive interference.
- at different speeds: Speed is not the condition; phase is.

options.label: C
options.content: with a path difference of one whole wavelength

questions.stem: Sound can be heard round a corner but light cannot be seen round it because
questions.explanation:
Sound wavelengths (about a metre) are comparable to doorways; light's wavelength is tiny, so it hardly diffracts.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sound travels faster than light: Light is far faster than sound.
- light cannot be reflected: Light reflects readily.
- sound is a transverse wave: Sound is longitudinal; this is not the reason.

options.label: D
options.content: the wavelength of sound is much longer, so it diffracts more

questions.stem: Water waves of frequency 4 Hz have a wavelength of 3 cm in deep water and travel at 9 cm s⁻¹ in shallow water. What is their wavelength in the shallow water?
questions.explanation:
The frequency is unchanged: $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{9}{4} = 2.25\ \text{cm}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 3 cm: The wavelength changes when the speed changes.
- 36 cm: You multiplied the speed by the frequency.
- 12 cm: That is the speed in deep water (4 × 3 = 12 cm s⁻¹).

papers.title: Sound Waves: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on sound waves, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In the bell-jar experiment, the sound of the bell fades as air is pumped out. This shows that sound
questions.explanation:
With the air removed, there is no medium to carry the vibrations, so the sound is not heard.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- travels faster in a vacuum: Sound cannot travel in a vacuum at all.
- is a transverse wave: The experiment says nothing about the type of wave.
- is produced by vibrations: The bell still vibrates; the point is that the sound cannot reach us.

options.label: A
options.content: needs a material medium to travel

questions.stem: A boy shouts 170 m from a cliff and hears the echo 1.0 s later. What is the speed of sound?
questions.explanation:
$v = \dfrac{2d}{t} = \dfrac{2 \times 170}{1.0} = 340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 170 m s⁻¹: The sound travels to the cliff and back: use 2d.
- 85 m s⁻¹: You halved instead of doubling.
- 680 m s⁻¹: You doubled twice.

questions.stem: Sound travels fastest in
questions.explanation:
Sound travels fastest in solids, where particles are closest and most tightly bound.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- air: Sound is slowest in gases.
- water: Sound is faster in water than in air, but slower than in steel.
- a vacuum: Sound cannot travel in a vacuum.

questions.stem: The pitch of a note depends on its
questions.explanation:
Higher frequency means higher pitch.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- amplitude: Amplitude decides loudness.
- overtones: Overtones decide quality (timbre).
- speed: All sounds in the same air travel at the same speed.

questions.stem: Two instruments play the same note at the same loudness but sound different because they differ in
questions.explanation:
Different instruments add different overtones to the fundamental, so the quality (timbre) differs.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- pitch: They play the same note, so their pitch (frequency) is the same.
- loudness: The loudness is the same.
- speed of sound: The speed is the same in the same air.

questions.stem: A ship sends a sound pulse to the sea bed and receives the echo after 0.6 s. If sound travels at 1500 m s⁻¹ in water, how deep is the sea?
questions.explanation:
$d = \dfrac{vt}{2} = \dfrac{1500 \times 0.6}{2} = 450\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 900 m: That is the total distance travelled, there and back.
- 2500 m: You divided the speed by the time.
- 225 m: You halved twice.

questions.stem: The range of frequencies audible to a normal human ear is about
questions.explanation:
Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20 kHz; above is ultrasound, below is infrasound.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2 Hz to 2000 Hz: The upper limit is about 20 kHz.
- 200 Hz to 200 000 Hz: 200 kHz is far into the ultrasound range.
- 20 kHz to 200 kHz: That is ultrasound, inaudible to humans.

questions.stem: The pitch of an ambulance siren seems higher as it approaches and lower as it moves away. This is the
questions.explanation:
Relative motion of source and listener changes the observed frequency: the Doppler effect.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- echo effect: An echo is a reflected sound.
- resonance effect: Resonance is vibration at the natural frequency.
- interference effect: Interference needs two coherent sources.

papers.title: Resonance and Musical Acoustics: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on resonance and musical acoustics, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A pipe closed at one end is 0.25 m long. If the speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹, what is its fundamental frequency (ignore the end correction)?
questions.explanation:
Closed pipe: $f_0 = \dfrac{v}{4L} = \dfrac{340}{1.0} = 340\ \text{Hz}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 680 Hz: That is the fundamental of an open pipe, $v/2L$.
- 1360 Hz: You used $v/L$.
- 85 Hz: You multiplied by L instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A stretched string vibrates at 200 Hz. What is its frequency if its tension is increased to four times the original, with length unchanged?
questions.explanation:
$f \propto \sqrt{T}$: $f = 200 \times \sqrt{4} = 400\ \text{Hz}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 800 Hz: Frequency is proportional to the square root of tension, not the tension.
- 100 Hz: Increasing tension raises the frequency.
- 50 Hz: Increasing tension raises the frequency.

questions.stem: A string 0.6 m long is fixed at both ends. What is the wavelength of its fundamental mode?
questions.explanation:
Fundamental: $L = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \Rightarrow \lambda = 2 \times 0.6 = 1.2\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.6 m: The fundamental has one loop: L = λ/2, so λ = 2L.
- 0.3 m: You halved the length.
- 2.4 m: That is 4L, the closed-pipe relation.

questions.stem: In a resonance-tube experiment with a 500 Hz fork, the first and second resonance lengths are 16 cm and 50 cm. What is the speed of sound?
questions.explanation:
$\dfrac{\lambda}{2} = L_2 - L_1 = 34$ cm, so $\lambda = 0.68$ m; $v = f\lambda = 500 \times 0.68 = 340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 170 m s⁻¹: You used λ = L₂ − L₁; the difference is half a wavelength.
- 660 m s⁻¹: You added the lengths instead of subtracting.
- 320 m s⁻¹: You used 4 × 16 cm as the wavelength (ignoring the end correction).

questions.stem: A pipe closed at one end can produce
questions.explanation:
With a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, only odd multiples of f₀ fit.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- only even harmonics: A closed pipe gives f₀, 3f₀, 5f₀, …
- all harmonics: That is true of an open pipe.
- no harmonics: It produces its fundamental and odd harmonics.

questions.stem: Shortening the vibrating length of a guitar string (tension unchanged)
questions.explanation:
Pressing a string against a fret shortens it and raises its frequency.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- lowers the pitch: Frequency is inversely proportional to length.
- does not change the pitch: The length law says f ∝ 1/L.
- makes the note louder only: It changes the frequency.

questions.stem: Transverse waves travel at 240 m s⁻¹ on a string 0.8 m long fixed at both ends. What is the fundamental frequency?
questions.explanation:
$f_0 = \dfrac{v}{2L} = \dfrac{240}{1.6} = 150\ \text{Hz}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 300 Hz: You used $v/L$; the fundamental is $v/2L$.
- 75 Hz: You used $v/4L$, the closed-pipe formula.
- 192 Hz: You multiplied v by L.

questions.stem: In a sonometer experiment, the paper rider on the wire is thrown off when
questions.explanation:
When the wire's natural frequency equals the fork's, it vibrates strongly (resonance) and throws off the rider.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the tension is reduced to zero: With no tension the wire cannot vibrate properly.
- the tuning fork is held far away: The fork's stem must touch the box.
- the wire is longer than 1 m: Length alone does not throw the rider off; matching frequency does.

options.label: A
options.content: the tension is reduced to zero

options.label: B
options.content: the tuning fork is held far away

options.label: C
options.content: the wire resonates with the tuning fork

options.label: D
options.content: the wire is longer than 1 m

papers.title: Light as a Wave: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on light as a wave, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The formation of shadows is evidence that light
questions.explanation:
An opaque object blocks the straight-line paths of light, leaving a shadow.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is a transverse wave: Shadows say nothing about the type of wave.
- can be polarised: Polarisation is shown with Polaroid filters.
- travels faster than sound: Shadows do not compare speeds.

questions.stem: An eclipse of the Sun occurs when
questions.explanation:
The Moon's shadow falls on the Earth: a solar eclipse.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon: That causes an eclipse of the Moon.
- the Sun comes between the Earth and the Moon: The Sun cannot come between them.
- the Moon is full: A solar eclipse happens at new moon.

options.label: A
options.content: the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth

options.label: B
options.content: the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon

options.label: C
options.content: the Sun comes between the Earth and the Moon

questions.stem: A pinhole camera is 20 cm long. A tree 12 m tall is 40 m from the pinhole. What is the height of the image?
questions.explanation:
$h_i = h_o \times \dfrac{v}{u} = 12 \times \dfrac{0.20}{40} = 0.06\ \text{m} = 6\ \text{cm}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 60 cm: You used 4 m instead of 40 m.
- 0.06 cm: That is the height in metres (0.06 m); the answer is wanted in centimetres.
- 2400 cm: You multiplied instead of using the ratio of distances.

questions.stem: The image formed by a pinhole camera is
questions.explanation:
Rays from the top of the object go to the bottom of the screen: a real, inverted image.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- virtual and upright: The image can be caught on the screen, so it is real; it is upside down.
- virtual and inverted: It is real, not virtual.
- real and upright: Rays cross at the pinhole, so the image is inverted.

questions.stem: Enlarging the hole of a pinhole camera makes the image
questions.explanation:
More light gets in, but each point of the object makes a patch rather than a point, so images overlap and blur.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- dimmer and sharper: A larger hole lets in more light.
- brighter and sharper: Overlapping images from the wider hole make it blurred.
- disappear: An image is still formed.

questions.stem: Light from the Sun takes 500 s to reach the Earth. If the speed of light is 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, what is the Sun–Earth distance?
questions.explanation:
$d = vt = 3.0 \times 10^{8} \times 500 = 1.5 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 3 × 10¹¹ m: You doubled the distance; the light travels it only once.
- 15 × 10¹¹ m: Check the power of ten: 3 × 10⁸ × 500 = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m, not 1.5 × 10¹² m.
- 0.15 × 10¹¹ m: Check the power of ten: 3 × 10⁸ × 500 = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m, not 1.5 × 10¹⁰ m.

questions.stem: In a double-slit experiment, the slits are 0.4 mm apart and the screen is 2.0 m away. The fringe spacing is 3.0 mm. What is the wavelength of the light?
questions.explanation:
$\lambda = \dfrac{yd}{D} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.4 \times 10^{-3}}{2.0} = 6.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 24 × 10⁻⁷ m: You multiplied by D instead of dividing.
- 12 × 10⁻⁷ m: You forgot to divide by D = 2.0 m.
- 60 × 10⁻⁷ m: You used d = 4 mm instead of 0.4 mm.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a luminous object?
questions.explanation:
A luminous object produces its own light.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Moon: The Moon reflects sunlight; it makes no light of its own.
- a mirror: A mirror only reflects light.
- a sheet of paper: Paper is seen by reflected light.

papers.title: Reflection of Light: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on reflection of light, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The image formed by a plane mirror is
questions.explanation:
Plane-mirror images are virtual, upright, the same size, as far behind as the object is in front, and laterally inverted.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- real, inverted and the same size: A plane mirror's image cannot be formed on a screen; it is virtual and upright.
- virtual, inverted and magnified: It is upright and the same size.
- real, upright and diminished: It is virtual and the same size.

options.label: A
options.content: real, inverted and the same size

options.label: C
options.content: virtual, upright and the same size as the object

questions.stem: Two plane mirrors are inclined at 60° to each other. How many images of an object between them are formed?
questions.explanation:
$n = \dfrac{360}{\theta} - 1 = \dfrac{360}{60} - 1 = 5$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 6: You forgot to subtract 1: n = 360/θ − 1.
- 3: That is the number for mirrors at 90°.
- 7: That is the number for mirrors at 45°.

questions.stem: A plane mirror is rotated through 12° while the incident ray stays fixed. Through what angle does the reflected ray turn?
questions.explanation:
The reflected ray turns through 2θ = 2 × 12° = 24°.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 12 °: The reflected ray turns through twice the angle of the mirror.
- 6 °: You halved instead of doubling.
- 168 °: You subtracted from 180°.

questions.stem: A ray strikes a plane mirror at a glancing angle of 35° to the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.explanation:
The angle of incidence (from the normal) is 90° − 35° = 55°, so the angle of reflection is 55°.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 35 °: Angles are measured from the normal, not from the mirror.
- 70 °: You doubled the glancing angle.
- 110 °: That is the angle between the incident and reflected rays.

questions.stem: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. How far from the mirror is the image?
questions.explanation:
$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{2}{30} \Rightarrow v = 15\ \text{cm}$ (real, in front of the mirror).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 20 cm: You subtracted f from u.
- 7.5 cm: You added 1/u and 1/f instead of subtracting.
- 40 cm: You added u and f.

questions.stem: A convex mirror is used as a driving mirror because it
questions.explanation:
The diminished, upright image lets the driver see a wide stretch of road behind.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- gives a magnified image: A convex mirror always gives a diminished image.
- gives a real image: Its images are virtual.
- focuses light to a point: That describes a concave mirror.

options.label: D
options.content: gives an upright image and a wide field of view

questions.stem: To obtain a virtual, upright, magnified image with a concave mirror, the object must be placed
questions.explanation:
Inside F, the reflected rays diverge and appear to come from a magnified image behind the mirror (shaving mirror).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- at the centre of curvature: That gives a real, inverted, same-size image.
- beyond the centre of curvature: That gives a real, inverted, diminished image.
- at the principal focus: Then the reflected rays are parallel and no image forms.

options.label: A
options.content: between the principal focus and the mirror

questions.stem: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 36 cm. What is its focal length?
questions.explanation:
$f = \dfrac{r}{2} = \dfrac{36}{2} = 18\ \text{cm}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 72 cm: f = r/2, not 2r.
- 36 cm: That is the radius of curvature.
- 9 cm: You divided by 4.

papers.title: Refraction and Total Internal Reflection: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on refraction and total internal reflection, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A ray of light enters glass from air at an angle of incidence of 30°. The angle of refraction is 19°. What is the refractive index of the glass?
questions.explanation:
$n = \dfrac{\sin 30°}{\sin 19°} = \dfrac{0.500}{0.326} = 1.54$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.58: Snell's law uses the sines of the angles, not the angles themselves.
- 0.65: You inverted the ratio; n = sin i / sin r.
- 0.92: Use sines, not cosines.

questions.stem: The refractive index of water is 4/3. A coin at the bottom of a pond 1.2 m deep appears to be how deep?
questions.explanation:
Apparent depth $= \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{n} = \dfrac{1.2}{4/3} = 0.9\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.6 m: You multiplied by n; apparent depth = real depth ÷ n.
- 0.3 m: That is the apparent displacement (1.2 − 0.9).
- 1.2 m: Refraction makes the coin look shallower.

questions.stem: The speed of light in a glass is 2.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. If its speed in air is 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, what is the refractive index of the glass?
questions.explanation:
$n = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{2.0 \times 10^{8}} = 1.5$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.667: You inverted the ratio; n = speed in air ÷ speed in glass.
- 5: You added the speeds.
- 1: You subtracted the speeds.

questions.stem: What is the critical angle for a glass of refractive index 1.5?
questions.explanation:
$\sin c = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{1}{1.5} = 0.667 \Rightarrow c = 41.8°$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 48.2 °: You used cos c = 1/n; the relation is sin c = 1/n.
- 33.7 °: You used tan c = 1/n.
- 60.0 °: You divided 90° by n.

questions.stem: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels from
questions.explanation:
TIR needs a denser-to-less-dense boundary and an angle of incidence above the critical angle.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- air to glass at any angle: TIR needs light going from a denser to a less dense medium.
- glass to air at an angle less than the critical angle: Below the critical angle the light refracts out.
- air to water at a large angle: Air is less dense than water; TIR cannot happen this way.

options.label: A
options.content: air to glass at any angle

options.label: B
options.content: glass to air at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle

options.label: C
options.content: glass to air at an angle less than the critical angle

options.label: D
options.content: air to water at a large angle

questions.stem: Optical fibres carry light signals over long distances by
questions.explanation:
Light strikes the core-cladding boundary above the critical angle and is totally reflected along the fibre.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- diffraction: Diffraction would spread the light out.
- dispersion: Dispersion separates colours; it is unwanted in fibres.
- refraction out of the fibre: Light that escapes is lost; the fibre keeps it inside by TIR.

questions.stem: A mirage on a hot road is caused by
questions.explanation:
Light from the sky bends gradually in the hot, less dense air near the road until it is totally internally reflected upwards.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- reflection from water on the road: There is no water; the 'pool' is an image of the sky.
- diffraction of sunlight: Diffraction is not the cause.
- dispersion in the hot air: The effect is not due to colour separation.

options.label: A
options.content: reflection from water on the road

options.label: D
options.content: refraction and total internal reflection in layers of air of different density

questions.stem: Light passes from air into water (refractive index 1.33) at an angle of incidence of 50°. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation:
$\sin r = \dfrac{\sin 50°}{1.33} = \dfrac{0.766}{1.33} = 0.576 \Rightarrow r = 35.2°$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 37.6 °: You divided the angle by n; divide sin i by n.
- 50 °: Light bends towards the normal entering water.
- 40 °: That is 90° − 50°; use Snell's law with the sines of the angles.

papers.title: Lenses and Image Formation: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on lenses and image formation, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: An object is placed 15 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. How far from the lens is the image?
questions.explanation:
$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{1}{30} \Rightarrow v = 30\ \text{cm}$ (real image).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5 cm: You subtracted f from u.
- 6 cm: You added 1/u and 1/f instead of subtracting.
- 25 cm: You added u and f.

questions.stem: What is the power of a converging lens of focal length 25 cm?
questions.explanation:
$P = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{0.25\ \text{m}} = +4\ \text{D}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 25 D: Power uses the focal length in metres: 1 ÷ 0.25.
- 0.04 D: Convert 25 cm to 0.25 m before taking the reciprocal.
- -4 D: A converging lens has positive power.

questions.stem: A diverging lens always forms an image that is
questions.explanation:
Rays leaving a diverging lens spread out, appearing to come from a smaller, upright image on the object side.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- real, inverted and diminished: A diverging lens cannot form a real image of a real object.
- virtual, upright and magnified: Its images are always smaller than the object.
- real, upright and magnified: Its images are virtual and diminished.

questions.stem: A converging lens is used as a magnifying glass. The object must be placed
questions.explanation:
Inside F, a converging lens gives a virtual, upright, magnified image.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- at 2F: That gives a real, same-size image.
- beyond 2F: That gives a real, diminished image (a camera).
- between F and 2F: That gives a real, magnified image (a projector).

options.label: B
options.content: between the lens and its principal focus

questions.stem: An object 5 cm tall is 30 cm from a converging lens and its image is formed 60 cm from the lens. How tall is the image?
questions.explanation:
$m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{60}{30} = 2$; image height $= 2 \times 5 = 10\ \text{cm}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2.5 cm: You inverted the magnification; m = v/u = 2.
- 2 cm: That is the magnification, not the image height.
- 300 cm: You multiplied the height by the image distance.

questions.stem: An object is placed 6 cm from a converging lens of focal length 12 cm. Where is the image? (real-is-positive convention)
questions.explanation:
$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{6} = -\dfrac{1}{12} \Rightarrow v = -12\ \text{cm}$: virtual, on the same side as the object.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 12 cm: The image is virtual, so its distance is negative.
- 4 cm: You added 1/u and 1/f.
- 6 cm: That is the object distance.

questions.stem: In a camera, the object is usually placed
questions.explanation:
A camera forms a real, inverted, diminished image of distant objects (beyond 2F).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- between F and the lens: That gives a virtual image, which cannot be recorded on film.
- at F: Then no image forms on the film.
- between F and 2F: That gives a magnified image, as in a projector.

questions.stem: A lens has a power of −2.5 D. What is its focal length?
questions.explanation:
$f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{-2.5} = -0.4\ \text{m} = -40\ \text{cm}$ (a diverging lens).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 40 cm: Negative power means a diverging lens with negative focal length.
- -0.4 cm: That is the focal length in metres, not centimetres.
- -25 cm: 1 ÷ 2.5 = 0.4 m = 40 cm, not 25 cm.

papers.title: Optical Instruments: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on optical instruments, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Short sight (myopia) is corrected by using a
questions.explanation:
A diverging lens spreads the rays so they focus on the retina instead of in front of it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- converging (convex) lens: That corrects long sight.
- cylindrical lens: That corrects astigmatism.
- plane glass: Plane glass does not change focus.

questions.stem: The part of the eye that controls the amount of light entering it is the
questions.explanation:
The iris changes the size of the pupil.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- retina: The retina detects light.
- cornea: The cornea refracts light.
- optic nerve: The optic nerve carries signals to the brain.

questions.stem: The eye focuses on objects at different distances by
questions.explanation:
Accommodation: the ciliary muscles change the lens's shape and so its focal length.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- moving the lens backwards and forwards: That is how a camera focuses.
- changing the size of the pupil: The pupil controls the amount of light.
- moving the retina: The retina does not move.

options.label: A
options.content: moving the lens backwards and forwards

options.label: B
options.content: changing the thickness of its lens

options.label: C
options.content: changing the size of the pupil

questions.stem: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 90 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 3 cm. What is its magnifying power in normal adjustment?
questions.explanation:
$M = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = \dfrac{90}{3} = 30$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 270: You multiplied the focal lengths.
- 0.033: You inverted the ratio; M = f_o / f_e.
- 93: That is the length of the telescope in cm, f_o + f_e.

questions.stem: A magnifying glass of focal length 5 cm forms an image at the near point, 25 cm from the eye. What is the magnification?
questions.explanation:
$m = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f} = 1 + \dfrac{25}{5} = 6$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5: You used D/f only; with the image at the near point, m = 1 + D/f.
- 0.2: You divided f by D.
- 30: You added D and f.

questions.stem: In a slide projector, the slide is placed upside down because the projection lens
questions.explanation:
The image on the screen is inverted relative to the slide, so an inverted slide gives an upright picture.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- forms a virtual image: A projector forms a real image on the screen.
- forms an upright image: A single converging lens forms an inverted real image.
- reflects the light: The lens refracts light.

questions.stem: Compared with the objective of an astronomical telescope, the objective of a compound microscope has a
questions.explanation:
A microscope objective has a very short focal length so that a tiny nearby object gives a large real image.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- much longer focal length: A telescope objective has the long focal length.
- larger diameter: Telescope objectives are made large to gather light.
- negative power: Both objectives are converging lenses.

questions.stem: Long sight (hypermetropia) occurs because the image of a near object is formed
questions.explanation:
The eyeball is too short or the lens too weak, so near objects focus behind the retina; a converging lens corrects it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- in front of the retina: That happens in short sight.
- on the blind spot: The blind spot is unrelated.
- at the pupil: Images form on (or near) the retina, not at the pupil.

papers.title: Dispersion and the Electromagnetic Spectrum: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on dispersion and the electromagnetic spectrum, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: When white light passes through a prism, the colour deviated most is
questions.explanation:
Glass has the highest refractive index for violet, so violet bends most.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- red: Red is deviated least.
- green: Green lies in the middle of the spectrum.
- yellow: Yellow is deviated less than violet.

questions.stem: A red shirt viewed in pure green light appears
questions.explanation:
A red object reflects only red; in green light it reflects nothing and looks black.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- red: There is no red light for it to reflect.
- green: The shirt absorbs green light.
- white: It reflects none of the green light.

questions.stem: Adding red and green light gives
questions.explanation:
In additive mixing of light, red + green = yellow.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- white: White needs red, green and blue together.
- cyan: Cyan is green + blue.
- magenta: Magenta is red + blue.

questions.stem: Which electromagnetic radiation has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation:
In order of increasing wavelength: gamma, X-rays, UV, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- gamma rays: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength.
- X-rays: X-rays have very short wavelengths.
- infrared: Infrared is longer than visible light but much shorter than radio waves.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a property of all electromagnetic waves?
questions.explanation:
Electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum; they need no medium.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- They travel at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum.  
  This is true of all electromagnetic waves.
- They are transverse waves.  
  This is true of all electromagnetic waves.
- They carry energy.  
  This is true of all electromagnetic waves.

options.label: A
options.content: They travel at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum.

options.label: B
options.content: They need a material medium to travel.

questions.stem: Microwaves used by a mobile phone have a frequency of 1.5 × 10⁹ Hz. What is their wavelength? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
$\lambda = \dfrac{c}{f} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.5 \times 10^{9}} = 0.2\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5 m: You divided the frequency by the speed.
- 2 m: Check the powers of ten: 3 × 10⁸ ÷ 1.5 × 10⁹ = 0.2.
- 4.5 m: You multiplied instead of dividing (and dropped powers of ten).

questions.stem: Ultraviolet lamps are used in banks to
questions.explanation:
Genuine notes carry marks that glow (fluoresce) under ultraviolet light.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- heat the building: Infrared is used for heating.
- send signals to satellites: Microwaves are used for satellite links.
- take images of bones: X-rays are used for that.

questions.stem: The colours of white light can be recombined by
questions.explanation:
An inverted prism reverses the dispersion and recombines the colours into white light (as does a spinning Newton's disc).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- passing it through a red filter: A filter removes colours; it does not recombine them.
- reflecting it from a black surface: A black surface absorbs the light.
- passing it through a narrow slit: A slit does not recombine colours.

options.label: A
options.content: passing it through a red filter

options.label: B
options.content: reflecting it from a black surface

options.label: C
options.content: passing it through a narrow slit

options.label: D
options.content: passing the spectrum through a second, inverted prism
